## 1. Rental rates are not behaving like a glut

Prices for last-generation silicon are at or near record levels, and have held there for months.

If compute were being overbuilt, the first place it would show is the rental market. It has not. On our reading of the daily rental indices, rates across the A100, H100, H200 and B200 are up roughly 30% year to date and have sustained those levels rather than spiking and fading. Silicon Data's B200 benchmark rose 24.4% in the first quarter alone, and the H200 neocloud rate rose 14.4% between early May and late July 2026 while the H100 rose 7.0%. The H100, note, being a chip two architectures from the frontier.

The distinction that matters is between tiers. Hyperscaler H100 pricing has been close to flat, anchored to long-dated capacity commitments, while the neocloud tier, where marginal demand actually clears has moved double digits. Bears quoting flat hyperscaler list prices as evidence of softening demand are reading the least informative series in the market.

The market is also institutionalising. CME will launch futures on Nvidia GPU rental rates on 5 October 2026, which turns compute into a hedgeable asset class and, for our purposes, produces a forward curve — the first observable, market-priced view of whether the glut everyone is forecasting actually arrives.

results.title: Together AI Cuts GPU Cluster Pricing in Half for Interruptible Workloads | Superpower Daily
highlights:
Together AI is opening a public preview that cuts the price of certain GPU capacity in half. Its new preemptible option runs NVIDIA GPU nodes at 50% of the on-demand rate, using spare capacity for workloads that can tolerate interruption. The trade-off is straightforward: Together can reclaim those nodes when it needs the capacity elsewhere. Affected Kubernetes pods receive a termination signal and get up to five minutes to checkpoint—that is, save enough progress to resume later—and exit before the node disappears. Together says the rate is fixed, rather than changing like a spot-market price, and usage is measured roughly every one to two minutes, so short jobs are billed for approximately the time they actually run. This works inside a normal Together GPU Cluster, not as a separate cluster. Customers must keep at least one standard node, while preemptible nodes can be added to new or existing clusters. Together can refill the requested preemptible capacity as spare capacity returns, but that target is not a reservation: live allocation may fall below it, and there is no minimum node lifetime. The model fits experiments, evaluations, fine-tuning, distillation, batch inference, and other restartable work. It is a poor match for multi-day jobs without checkpoints or strict serving without fallback. Kubernetes is supported in every region for now; Slurm, more regions, and in-place conversion are planned. The key constraint is whether a team’s software can make a sudden GPU loss routine instead of disruptive.

Together recommends the capacity for short experiments, evaluations, fine-tuning, distillation, batch inference and other work that can resume from a checkpoint, retry or requeue. These examples use mid-range specialty cloud rates. Your actual cost depends on region, configuration, and commitment length.

...

## H100 vs H200 vs B200 – Which GPU Should You Rent?

### H100 vs H200 gpu rental comparison: What the Numbers Mean in Practice

Three NVIDIA options dominate the high-end rental market. Most comparison guides treat them neutrally. That doesn’t help you make a decision, so this one won’t.

| Spec | H100 SXM5 | H200 SXM5 | B200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Architecture | Hopper | Hopper+ | Blackwell |
| VRAM | 80GB HBM3 | 141GB HBM3e | 192GB HBM3e |
| Memory Bandwidth | 3.35 TB/s | 4.8 TB/s | 8.0 TB/s |
| FP8 Throughput | 1,979 TFLOPS | 1,979 TFLOPS | 4,500+ TFLOPS |
| Typical Rental Price/hr | $2.20 – $3.00 | $3.50 – $4.80 | $5.50 – $8.00+ |
| Cloud Availability | Good | Limited | Very Limited |

Pick the H100 when you are training models up to 70B parameters, fine-tuning pre-trained weights on custom data, running inference where the model fits in 80GB of VRAM, or when you simply need the instance to start without sitting on a waitlist. PyTorch, JAX, vLLM, and TensorRT-LLM have all been tuned for it. That matters for production workloads.

Pick the H200 when your model or inference workload doesn’t fit in 80GB of VRAM. That’s the main reason to choose it. The H200 comes with 141GB of HBM3e memory, which means you don’t need to split a large model across multiple H100s. That simplifies your setup and can save money overall, even though the H200 costs more per GPU. Mixture-of-experts models and long-context inference workloads are where it delivers real value.

Pick the B200 when you absolutely need maximum rated throughput, you’ve built a long-term plan around Blackwell, and you’ve got verified technology. That last point isn’t a minor caveat. Outside top-tier cloud agreements, B200 inventory is genuinely hard to secure in 2026.

Honest bottom line: for most teams, H100 gpu cloud is still the right call. H200 and B200 premiums only make sense in specific, well-defined scenarios. Don’t pay for capability your workload won’t use.

results.title: Wall Street Can Price a GPU Hour. Your Business Still Has to Price the Work. | by The Ai Consultancy | Sep, 2026 | Medium
highlights:
Share
Press enter or click to view image in full size
A balance holds a computing component and a stack of blank documents against a data centre background.
A cloud invoice and a commodity market seem to belong to different departments. One arrives with the software bills. The other concerns traders, exchanges and contracts whose details most business owners are content to leave alone. Compute futures bring those worlds closer together by offering a financial reference for the cost of the infrastructure on which AI depends.
The idea is understandable. A company building a data centre faces uncertainty about what customers will pay for its capacity. A company buying large amounts of computing power faces uncertainty about its future cost. A market tied to a recognised price index can give both sides another way to manage that exposure.
CME plans to launch its compute futures on 5 October 2026, pending regulatory review. Its proposed contracts track Silicon Data rental indices for Nvidia H100 and B200 GPUs. ICE has separately announced planned contracts with Ornn, also subject to regulatory approval. These are plans for new markets, with their practical usefulness still to be established.
For an SME using AI to serve customers or process documents, the most useful implication is a sharper question about its own bill. A public benchmark may improve visibility into one input. The business still needs to understand how that input becomes an acceptable piece of work, and which costs appear along the way.
## A reference price is an important but limited achievement
Computing capacity has several characteristics that make a common price useful. Differences in hardware and location can make offers hard to compare, especially when their access terms vary. Providers commit money before they know exactly how demand will develop. A reference index can give participants a shared starting point for negotiation and financial risk management.
CME’s planned contracts relate to rental-price indices for particular GPU types. ICE says its planned products will be denominated in US dollars and settled in cash. Under a cash-settled arrangement, the financial result is determined by the contract’s settlement rules. It does not itself deliver a reserved machine in the region where a business needs to run its application.
That distinction separates price exposure from service availability. A financial position might offset some movement in a benchmark while the underlying computing service remains unavailable or unsuitable. The business still needs an operating supplier able to provide suitable capacity when required. Financial settlement does not perform those operational tasks.
The oil comparison, used in Reuters Breakingviews’ discussion of the market, captures part of the attraction. A widely recognised benchmark can help participants plan around a critical input. The comparison becomes less useful when it encourages buyers to treat all nominally similar computing capacity as interchangeable.
An hour on a particular chip can support different amounts of useful work depending on the surrounding system. The software configuration and surrounding infrastructure affect throughput. So do the workload’s requirements and the number of requests being processed at once. A business needs to understand these differences before assuming that a cheaper nominal hour produces a cheaper service.
Location introduces further conditions. A region may matter because of latency, contractual commitments or the organisation’s data arrangements. Capacity available elsewhere may have limited practical value. A benchmark that combines transactions across a wider market can be informative while remaining an imperfect match for the buyer’s specific requirement.
This mismatch is often described as basis risk: the exposure a business actually faces may move differently from the benchmark used to manage it. The concept is useful even for a company that never trades a derivative. It reminds the buyer to ask whether the reference price describes the service it is purchasing closely enough to support the conclusion being drawn.
## The AI bill contains more than the machinery
Many SMEs buy a software application or a model service rather than renting GPUs directly. Their price may be expressed per user, per request or per unit of model usage. Between that price and the underlying hardware sit other costs, together with the supplier’s commercial decisions. A change in GPU rental prices does not establish an equivalent change in the customer’s invoice.
The supplier may develop the model and manage the infrastructure, with customer support included in the service. Integration work and contractual service commitments can add further value. Its own capacity may have been purchased under long-term arrangements. The relationship between an observed spot price and the service’s current cost can therefore be indirect.
There is nothing unusual about a supplier charging for more than its raw input. Businesses buy outcomes and operating convenience in many markets. The problem arises when a customer uses one input price as though it describes the complete economics, or when a supplier cites infrastructure costs without explaining which part of the service they actually affect.
The more useful comparison begins with the unit of work the business cares about. For a document-processing workflow, that might be an accepted record entered correctly into the target system. For customer support, it might be a resolved request that meets the agreed service standard. The definition needs enough detail to prevent an incomplete or low-quality output being counted as success.
Once that outcome is defined, the business can include the costs required to produce it. Model usage is one part. Retrieval and integration may add others. Human review and correction can become substantial. A task that fails repeatedly may consume resources without adding to the number of accepted outcomes. Measuring only the first model response misses that work.
Take a deliberately simplified hypothetical example. A workflow costs £100 to run against 1,000 records, but only 800 pass the agreed checks without further work. Its initial processing cost is 12.5 pence per accepted record, before review and correction costs. Dividing by all submitted records would give 10 pence and hide the effect of the unsuccessful cases.
The arithmetic is elementary, which is part of its value. It makes the denominator visible. A more complex service can use the same discipline while accounting for partial completions and different kinds of work. The business should know whether a claimed saving relates to attempted tasks, completed outputs or outcomes accepted by the people who rely on them.
Unused capacity complicates the comparison further. A dedicated environment can offer control and predictable access while spending part of the day idle. Its cost still belongs to the service. A shared or usage-based route may spread that burden differently, although the customer then accepts the associated service terms. The relevant question is how much of the purchased capacity produces work at the times the business needs it.
This is why a short, busy demonstration can overstate the economics of a permanent installation. The test may keep the equipment occupied continuously while ordinary demand arrives unevenly. A realistic budget should include quiet periods and the capacity retained for peaks. The resulting unit cost may still be attractive, but it will reflect the business’s actual pattern of use.
## Cheap usage can become expensive activity
A fall in unit prices can encourage a team to use more AI. Larger batches and longer context can increase consumption. Teams may also give an agent more attempts at difficult work. Some of that expansion will produce useful work that was previously uneconomic. Some may add little value. The invoice reflects the combined effect of price and behaviour.

This creates an operating challenge that a market benchmark cannot resolve. The business needs to decide when additional attempts are worthwhile. A service that keeps working until it produces an acceptable result may be valuable in one context and wasteful in another. The permitted effort should relate to the value of the task and the available alternative.
Consider a hypothetical team extracting basic fields from routine documents. When a document is damaged or unusual, the system could spend increasingly large amounts of computation trying to interpret it. Sending the exception to a person may be cheaper and more reliable. A well-designed workflow recognises that boundary and records why the task was handed over.
The same analysis can favour more expensive computation. A stronger model may resolve complex cases with fewer attempts or reduce the amount of human correction. Its usage rate can be higher while the cost per accepted outcome is lower. The relevant comparison follows the complete route from input to approved result.
Quality needs to remain part of that comparison over time. A price reduction achieved by changing the model or reducing its effort may alter error patterns. A business should check whether apparent savings survive the cost of rework and the consequences of mistakes. The baseline should include both cost and the standard of work delivered.
Demand can change independently of the technology. ... Clearing an accumulated backlog can create another peak. ... Capacity planning therefore belongs beside unit-cost measurement.
For many SMEs, sensible controls will be operational. Set limits on work that can run unattended.

highlights:
# AI용 GPU 빌려준다…베슬AI, '엔비디아 B200' 1000장 이상 확보 

 최태범 기자 

 입력 2026.08.07 16:00 

수정 2026.08.13 04:40

[이 기사에 나온 스타트업에 대한 보다 다양한 기업정보는 유니콘팩토리 빅데이터 플랫폼 '데이터랩'에서 볼 수 있습니다.]

AI(인공지능) 인프라 기업 베슬AI가 엔비디아(NVIDIA)의 블랙웰 기반 GPU(그래픽처리장치) 'B200'을 1000장 이상 확보하고 이달부터 순차 공급한다고 7일 밝혔다. 

2020년 설립된 베슬AI는 AI 모델의 학습과 배포, 운영을 자동화하는 인프라 소프트웨어를 개발해 왔다. 최근에는 GPU 자원을 직접 조달해 공급하는 네오클라우드 사업으로 영역을 넓히고 있다. 

네오클라우드는 AI 연산에 특화한 GPU 자원을 빌려주는 사업자를 말한다. 범용 서버 중심의 기존 클라우드와 달리 고성능 GPU와 이를 구동할 개발·운영 환경을 묶어 제공해, 데이터센터를 직접 짓기 어려운 기업이 주로 이용한다. 

블랙웰은 엔비디아가 2024년 공개한 GPU 아키텍처로 이전 세대인 호퍼(Hopper)를 잇는다. B200은 이 아키텍처를 적용한 데이터센터용 GPU로 대규모 모델의 학습과 추론에 함께 쓰인다. 

베슬AI는 SK텔레콤(83,900원 ▲2,400 +2.94%)과의 협력을 통해 이번 물량을 확보했다. 확보한 B200은 자사 GPU 클라우드 서비스 '베슬 클라우드(VESSL Cloud)'에 반영해 국내외 고객에게 공급할 계획이다. 

베슬 클라우드는 복수의 글로벌 데이터센터를 기반으로 A100, H100, B200 등 고성능 GPU를 온디맨드·스팟·예약형으로 제공하는 서비스다. 기업과 연구자가 복잡한 인프라 구축 부담 없이 대규모 AI 모델의 학습과 추론에 필요한 컴퓨팅 자원을 유연하게 활용할 수 있도록 돕는다. 

베슬AI는 앞서 3월 엔비디아 'GB200'과 'B300'을 확보하며 라인업을 넓혔다. B300은 대규모 AI 모델 추론에, GB200은 초거대 모델 학습에 각각 쓰인다. 연내 GPU 1만장, 내년에는 5만장 규모의 100메가와트(MW)급 인프라를 갖추겠다는 목표를 세웠다.
